body.text: The 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila, which was held from 15 to 17 November, demonstrated ASEAN’s strengths and weaknesses. Amid a Middle East war that has pushed up regional fuel prices, leaders established new frameworks for digital trade, energy and critical minerals. Yet the summit’s most contentious issues remain unresolved: the South China Sea dispute, the civil war in Myanmar and the Thailand–Cambodia rift.

ASEAN can boast of some economic achievements. One of them is the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which was signed on 14 November and is ASEAN’s first standalone and legally binding digital pact. ASEAN also accelerated the entry into force of the upgraded ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) and ASEAN-China Free Trade Area 3.0, with the latter scheduled to take effect on 1 December. ASEAN and Canada announced the “substantive conclusion of negotiations” for a free trade agreement, making Canada ASEAN’s prospective first North American free trade partner.

Beyond trade, the Middle East shock added urgency to ASEAN’s longer-standing energy and resource security agenda. In Manila, all members signed the Enhanced MoU on the ASEAN Power Grid (APG), a framework to connect the region’s electricity networks. ASEAN members also reiterated support for the establishment of a regional stockpiling mechanism. This allows countries to access the fuel reserves of neighbouring countries during emergencies. In May, leaders urged the ratification of the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement to enable this mechanism (only six of eleven ASEAN members had ratified the agreement as of late October). Japan also proposed an Asia Oil Security Task Force while ASEAN and China launched an Energy Cooperation Partnership.
ASEAN’s convening power was also on display, but it cut both ways: great-power diplomacy showed that the bloc is more a venue than an agenda-setter.

However, the summit has less to show for in the security ledger. On maritime affairs, a Philippine priority, leaders built on the Maritime Cooperation declaration adopted in Cebu in May, which noted that all members are now parties to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), after Cambodia’s ratification in February. But the South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) missed the 2026 target set in 2023. Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said that China and ASEAN reached “provisional agreement” on about 80 per cent of the text. Only one of four milestone issues, the Code’s relationship with the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties, is settled; but the other issues — legal status, scope and terms of reference remain. The ASEAN-China joint statement noted that the Code is in a “final phase” — a position maintained since early this year. Statements since 2012 have noted that the Code had reached an “early conclusion”.

On Myanmar, ASEAN made a pragmatic move forward, albeit without resolution. ASEAN’s decision at the summit still restricted Myanmar’s participation at the bloc’s meetings to non-political representation. For the first time, however, the bloc set out “a phased and progress-based approach” under which ASEAN “may consider the gradual restoration” of full representation after “sustained and concrete progress”.

If Myanmar tests ASEAN’s principles, the Thailand–Cambodia rift tests its cohesion. The border conflict, frozen by a fragile ceasefire in July and a joint statement in December 2025, still resurfaced on the sidelines of the Manila Summit. There is a dilemma for ASEAN leaders here: Cambodia is seeking multilateral attention on the issue, while Thailand insists on settling it bilaterally, leaving ASEAN’s regional dispute-settlement mechanisms unused. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet stayed in Phnom Penh during the main ASEAN summit to host the Francophonie Summit, which voiced concern over the dispute. At the ASEAN–ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly (AIPA) interface, Cambodia reportedly secured language on the ceasefire, which said that the conflict has displaced 20,000 displaced people. This was despite objections from Thailand’s House Speaker.

ASEAN’s struggle to manage a dispute between two of its own members contrasts with the growing appeal of its founding principles to outsiders. On the eve of the summit, Cyprus, Slovakia and Slovenia acceded to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (TAC). They follow the paths made by Sweden, Poland, Romania and Lithuania in July. Significantly, all seven are EU members and middle or smaller powers — a sign that Europe, beyond its major capitals, now sees Southeast Asia as strategically relevant, and that ASEAN’s norms of non-interference and renunciation of force appeal to states seeking rules-based partners amid great-power rivalry. Yet the TAC binds more in symbolism than in practice. Russia, a party since 2004, invaded Ukraine — also a party since 2022; the ASEAN foreign ministers’ statement did not even name Russia.

ASEAN’s convening power was also on display, but it cut both ways: great-power diplomacy showed that the bloc is more a venue than an agenda-setter. On his way to Shenzhen for APEC and the Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting, US President Donald Trump appeared to treat the summit as a waypoint to other meetings. He arrived in Manila after the closing ceremony, for an US-ASEAN informal summit that produced anti-scam principles and a Comprehensive Work Plan for ASEAN-US cooperation in 2026–2030. This marked a contrast with Kuala Lumpur last year, when he arrived on the opening day of the ASEAN Summit for the formal ASEAN–US Summit. The Quad, meanwhile, met on the sidelines, endorsing ASEAN centrality while launching its own initiatives, including a first joint patrol-aircraft exercise in 2027.Policy Implications

These trends suggest three policy implications. First, ASEAN’s credibility rests on implementation, not new texts. For example, this means bringing DEFA into force and ratifying the petroleum agreement. Second, ASEAN needs concrete milestones on the security front. On the COC, the 2027 chair should focus negotiations on the hardest issues — legal status, geographical scope and terms of reference — while pressing for interim measures, such as an incident-at-sea hotline between coast guards. On Myanmar, senior officials should define what “sustained and concrete progress” means — for instance, a halt to air strikes on civilians or the release of political prisoners — before any restoration of political representation.Third, ASEAN should give its institutions the tools to act. For example, it should appoint the long-discussed longer-term Special Envoy on Myanmar with a multi-year mandate and adopt the proposed foreign ministers’ crisis coordination protocol.These tasks fall to Singapore, which chairs ASEAN in its 60th year under the theme “Deeper Integration, Wider Partnerships”. Its push towards a single ASEAN market with closer finance, digital and energy links maps neatly onto the implementation agenda, while wider partnerships suit a year marking 50 years of relations with the US, Canada and the EU. After all, economic resilience has bought ASEAN some time; internal cohesion will determine whether it lasts.
